title: A Telangana MBA Student Took a Pizza Delivery Shift. He Was Lured to a Vacant Apartment and Shot Dead.
excerpt: Anshul Kuncha, 28, was found with a gunshot wound to the head outside a Philadelphia housing complex. Police say the order was placed for an empty unit. No arrests have been made.
body:
Anshul Kuncha left his apartment in North Philadelphia on the night of June 6 to deliver three pizzas. He was working a weekend shift at Pete's Pizza, a part-time job he held alongside a position at a multinational company while pursuing an MBA in the United States. He was 28 years old, from Gundlapochampally in Medchal-Malkajgiri district, Telangana.

The order directed him to a unit in the Raymond Rosen Homes complex on Edgley Street. The apartment was vacant. Kuncha delivered the pizzas anyway — three boxes and a bag were later found inside the empty unit, untouched. Moments after he stepped back outside, he was shot in the head at close range.

Philadelphia police officers found him lying unresponsive in the courtyard shortly after 12:30 AM. Three spent shell casings were recovered inches from his body. He was rushed to Temple University Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

## A Suspected Trap

Chief Inspector Scott Small of the Philadelphia Police Department told reporters that the shooter or shooters stood "very, very close to the victim." Surveillance footage from the Philadelphia Housing Authority captured two individuals in dark clothing following Kuncha after he arrived at the complex. One carried a dark backpack. The shooting itself was not captured on camera.

Nothing was stolen from Kuncha — not his phone, not his wallet, not his delivery vehicle, which was found parked nearby with a pizza warmer still inside. The absence of robbery has deepened suspicions that the delivery order was used solely as a lure.

Police have the phone number used to place the order. No arrests have been made.

## A Pattern Delivery Workers Know Too Well

Kuncha's killing follows a grim pattern that delivery workers across American cities have come to fear. So-called trap orders — fake delivery requests designed to draw workers to isolated locations for robbery or assault — have been documented in cities including Philadelphia, Chicago, Houston, and Atlanta. Most go unreported. Few result in arrests.

What makes Kuncha's case particularly disturbing is that nothing was taken. If the motive was not robbery, investigators have offered no alternative explanation.

His family in Telangana told Indian media that Kuncha had been robbed once before in the United States — his chain, phone, and cash were taken in a prior incident. He had come to the US in 2023 after completing an engineering degree from a college in Hyderabad, and had been building a life: studying, working full-time during the week, and picking up delivery shifts on weekends to earn extra money.

## A Familiar Grief

The Indian Consulate General in New York confirmed his identity in a post on X. "We are deeply saddened by the untimely demise of Mr. Anshul Kuncha, an Indian national in Philadelphia, PA," it wrote. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences to his family during this difficult time."

Kuncha's death adds to a growing list of Indian students and workers killed in violent incidents across the United States in recent years. The pattern — young Indians in their twenties, often in cities far from home, working multiple jobs to fund their education — has become a recurring source of anguish for the diaspora community.

His family has requested repatriation of his remains. The investigation continues.

## The Broader Question

There are more than 300,000 Indian students currently enrolled in American universities, many of whom work part-time in gig economy and service jobs to cover tuition and living costs. Delivery work — through apps like DoorDash, Uber Eats, and Instacart, or directly for restaurants — is among the most common.

It is also among the most dangerous. The Bureau of Labor Statistics classifies delivery work as a higher-risk occupation, with workers regularly exposed to traffic hazards, late-night shifts, and increasingly, targeted violence. Yet the gig economy's structure offers little in the way of safety infrastructure: no dispatch protocols for suspicious orders, no panic buttons integrated into most ordering systems, and no employer-provided security training.

For the thousands of Indian students who depend on delivery work to make their American education possible, Kuncha's death is not an abstraction. It is a reminder that the gap between ambition and safety can be measured in a single fake order to an empty apartment.
